explanation: She never visited India, but in her old age she learned Hindustani from her Indian attendant, Abdul Karim.

claims.text: Queen Victoria took the title Empress of India in 1876, under the Royal Titles Act.
Elizabeth I, Elizabeth II and Anne never held the title Empress of India.
Queen Victoria learned Hindustani from her Indian attendant Abdul Karim.

evidence.restatement: The Royal Titles Act of 1876 let Victoria take the title Empress of India; she was proclaimed at the Delhi Durbar on 1 January 1877.

evidence.restatement: The title began with Victoria and was given up by George VI in 1948, so Elizabeth I, Anne and Elizabeth II never held it.
Queen Victoria never travelled to India.
From 1887 her Indian attendant Abdul Karim, the Munshi, taught Victoria Hindustani (Urdu).
The Royal Titles Act received assent in April 1876 and Victoria took the style Empress of India from 1 May 1876; the Delhi proclamation followed on 1 January 1877.

claimResults.note: Some books give 1877, the year of the Delhi proclamation. 1876 holds for the Act and her adoption of the title. High-risk claim: my knowledge check only counts once check A carries external evidence for it.

evidence.restatement: Anne and Elizabeth I reigned long before British rule in India, and Elizabeth II never used the title; her father George VI was the last to hold it.
From 1887 Victoria studied Hindustani with her Indian attendant Abdul Karim.

issues.note: A reader may know the Delhi proclamation date of 1 January 1877 and doubt 1876. The Royal Titles Act and her adoption of the style are 1876, which the claim says, so the key and the stem stand.
